plan.question: Mr. Brooks has fallen twice at night and started tamsulosin 6 days ago. Which tests will you use today, what does his medication list change about how you train him, and how will you keep him safe?

parts.label: Tests
parts.criteria: Chooses orthostatic vital signs (new alpha blocker, falls on getting up) and a few measures from the neurologic core set or the fall-risk screen (Berg, FGA, 10 meter Walk Test, TUG, five times sit-to-stand, ABC), knowing the fall-risk cut-offs (Berg under 50, TUG over 11 s, gait speed under 1.0 m/s, sit-to-stand over 12 s); does not spend the visit on every test.
parts.modelAnswer: Orthostatic vitals first, because of the new tamsulosin and the night-time falls. Then the Berg or FGA, the 10 meter Walk Test and the TUG: Berg under 50, TUG over 11 seconds or gait speed under 1.0 m/s mean fall risk.

parts.label: Training and safety
parts.criteria: Gait belt and guarding on the weak side for anything upright; stands him in stages after sitting, and sits him at once if light-headed; reports a new orthostatic drop with the new alpha blocker to his physician; walking training at moderate to high intensity guided by RPE because the beta blocker blunts his heart rate; not static standing balance to improve walking; a home program of challenging balance and walking at the guideline dose.
parts.modelAnswer: Gait belt on and guarding on the left whenever he is up; ankle pumps and standing in stages, and straight back to the chair if he is light-headed; call his physician about the orthostatic drop and the tamsulosin. Train walking fast with obstacles, setting intensity by RPE, since metoprolol blunts his heart rate. Home program: progressive, challenging balance and walking, at least 150 minutes to 3 hours a week for 6 to 12 months.

expertPath.text: Gait belt on. Orthostatic vital signs first: a 26/12 drop with light-headedness six days after tamsulosin.
Call his physician about the drop, the new tamsulosin and the night falls.
TUG 16 s, 10 meter Walk Test 0.62 m/s, Berg 41: high fall risk.
Ankle pumps, stand in stages, walk at his own pace, then fast walking with cones set by RPE (metoprolol blunts his heart rate). Check RPE; rest seated.
Home program: challenging balance and walking, at least 150 minutes to 3 hours a week for 6 to 12 months, and getting up slowly at night.

safePlan.headline: Tested, trained and safe
safePlan.body: You chose tests that answered his questions, found the orthostatic drop and called his physician, guarded him every time he stood, and trained his walking hard but by RPE. That is the expert path.

planGaps.headline: Safe, with gaps
planGaps.body: No fall, which matters most. Look at the gait belt, how long he stayed up light-headed, the call to his physician, how you set his intensity, and the home program's dose.

noWalking.headline: Safe, but no walking training
noWalking.body: Testing and safety were there; the training was not. Walking training at moderate to high intensity is what moves walking after stroke.

fell.headline: A fall in the clinic
fell.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. A gait belt and guarding on the weak side, standing in stages, and sitting him down at once when he is light-headed prevent this fall.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Choose the tests worth the time: three or four measures leave room for walking training in an hour.

scoring.modelReasoning: Two falls on getting up at night and a new alpha blocker (tamsulosin) on top of metoprolol and lisinopril make orthostatic hypotension the first thing to test: 26/12 with light-headedness meets the definition (20/10 within 3 min). Report it to his physician the same visit. Use a few measures from the core set and the fall-risk screen (TUG 16 s, gait speed 0.62 m/s, Berg 41: all past the cut-offs): high fall risk. Guard with a gait belt whenever he is up, stand him in stages, and sit him at once if light-headed. Train walking at moderate to high intensity with variable stepping, set by RPE because metoprolol blunts the heart rate response, rather than static standing balance. Home program: progressive, challenging balance and walking at least 150 minutes to 3 hours a week for 6 to 12 months.
